title.title: Introduction to Smart Contracts
title.subtitle: What a smart contract is, where the idea came from, and what it can and cannot do

warmup.heading: Bitcoin or Ethereum?
warmup.subtitle: Tag each statement as Bitcoin, Ethereum or both.

items.why: Bitcoin was the first blockchain. Ethereum came in 2015.

items.stmt: Launched in 2015 by Vitalik Buterin & co.
items.why: Ethereum mainnet went live July 2015 with the Solidity language.
Bitcoin has a fixed 21M supply. ETH has no hard cap (~120M circulating).
Ethereum runs arbitrary logic on the EVM. Bitcoin Script is intentionally limited.

items.stmt: Tracks funds with the UTXO model
items.why: Bitcoin spends discrete unspent outputs. Ethereum uses account balances.
Ethereum mutates a balance per account. Bitcoin uses UTXOs.

items.stmt: Switched to Proof of Stake in 2022
items.why: The Merge moved Ethereum to PoS. Bitcoin still uses Proof of Work.

items.stmt: A public, decentralised ledger where the native coin pays fees
items.why: True of both — BTC pays Bitcoin fees, ETH pays Ethereum gas.

cards.title: Addresses
cards.desc: Two kinds of account: people, controlled by a private key, and programs, controlled by their own code. A smart contract is the second kind.

cards.title: One shared computer
cards.desc: Thousands of independent machines run the same program and must agree on the result. That agreement is what makes the outcome trustworthy.

cards.title: Every action has a price
cards.desc: You pay a small fee for each step the network performs. That stops spam and runaway programs — and makes on-chain storage expensive.

cards.title: Signed instructions
cards.desc: A transaction is a signed instruction that changes the shared record. Only a person's key can start one; it can call a program.

recap.footerB: a smart contract. The rest of the course is about what that code can do and when it is the right tool.

what.heading: What is a Smart Contract?
what.subtitle: A program stored on a blockchain that runs exactly as written.
what.defLeadB: is a self-executing program stored on a blockchain whose terms are written directly in code — not in natural language.
what.defBody: When its conditions are met, the contract executes automatically, with no intermediary and no manual trigger.

compareRows.smart: Enforced by the network running it
Requires trust in the code only

compareRows.trad: Can be interpreted — and argued over

props.title: Autonomous
props.desc: Executes when conditions are met; nobody approves it after deployment.

props.title: Immutable
props.desc: Once deployed, the code cannot be changed.

props.title: Transparent
props.desc: Anyone can read the code on-chain; there are no hidden clauses.

props.title: Deterministic
props.desc: Same inputs always give the same output, so every node agrees on the result.

props.title: Trustless
props.desc: Parties need to trust the code, not each other.

history.heading: Historical Evolution of Smart Contracts
history.subtitle: From an idea with nothing to run it on to $100B+ in live contracts.

events.title: Szabo coins "smart contract"
events.desc: Promises enforced by code — the vending-machine analogy, 15 years before any chain could run it.

events.title: Bitcoin — first on-chain contracts
events.desc: Script does conditional spending (multisig, timelocks) — deliberately non-Turing-complete.

events.title: Ethereum + Solidity
events.desc: The Turing-complete EVM ships: deploy arbitrary contract logic to a shared, trustless computer.

events.title: The DAO — first contract crisis
events.desc: A reentrancy bug drains $60M; Ethereum forks (ETH/ETC). Security becomes a discipline.

events.title: ERC-20 — token contracts
events.desc: A shared token interface every wallet & exchange understands. The ICO boom follows.

events.title: ERC-721 — NFT contracts
events.desc: A standard for unique, owned tokens — the basis of NFTs, digital deeds and tickets.

events.title: DeFi Summer
events.desc: Contracts calling contracts — "money legos." Lending, trading & yield, no intermediary.

events.title: Audited, multi-chain, high-stakes
events.desc: $100B+ in contracts across chains; audits mandatory — $6B+ lost to exploits since 2016.

exercise.heading: Contract or not?
exercise.subtitle: Six everyday agreements. Could each run as code, or does it need a person or an institution?

scenarios.title: A vending machine
scenarios.desc: Insert coins, pick a snack, get it — or get your coins back.
scenarios.reason: Fixed rule, instant check, automatic delivery — Szabo's original smart contract.

scenarios.title: A Netflix subscription
scenarios.desc: Pay monthly for access to a video library run by one company.
scenarios.reason: One company runs the content, the servers and the rules — nothing needs trustless enforcement. A billing database wins.

scenarios.title: Escrow for a house sale
scenarios.desc: Buyer's money is held until the title transfer is confirmed, then released.
scenarios.reason: Funds move only when a verifiable condition is met — the textbook pattern (Propy does this today). The title itself still needs the land registry.

scenarios.title: A loyalty-points scheme
scenarios.desc: Earn points at one retailer, spend them at the same retailer.
scenarios.reason: A single issuer defines, prices and can cancel the points. It is their database — a blockchain adds cost, not trust.

scenarios.title: A court judgement
scenarios.desc: A judge decides who was at fault and what the compensation is.
scenarios.reason: Needs interpretation of facts, intent and fairness. Code executes; it does not judge.

scenarios.title: Flight-delay insurance payout
scenarios.desc: If your flight lands more than two hours late, you are paid automatically.
scenarios.reason: The delay is a public, checkable fact — an oracle reports it and the payout fires by itself (parametric insurance).

quiz.question: Nick Szabo introduced the concept of smart contracts in 1994. Which real-world object did he use as the foundational analogy to explain how they work?
options: A notary office — a trusted third party that validates and records agreements between parties.
A vending machine — a mechanism that autonomously enforces the terms of a transaction without a human intermediary.
A court of law — an authority that resolves disputes and enforces contractual obligations after the fact.
A bank vault — a secure system that holds assets until conditions agreed by both parties are met.
quiz.explanation: Szabo's analogy was the vending machine: insert money, select an item, and the machine checks the payment and delivers the product with no cashier and no dispute. His insight was that conditional logic enforced by a mechanism rather than a person could be built into digital protocols. Ethereum made that possible two decades later.

takeaways.title: Section 01 — Key Takeaways
items: A smart contract is self-executing code on a blockchain; once deployed, no single party can alter it
Nick Szabo described the concept in 1994; Bitcoin (2009) and Ethereum (2015) made it real
Key properties: autonomous, immutable, transparent, deterministic, trustless
Vending machine model: conditions met, automatic execution, no human judgement
Not a legal contract, not smart, not free, not unstoppable; the value is removing middlemen, locking rules and settling fast
DeFi, NFTs and DAOs are all smart contracts; $6B+ lost to exploits shows the same code enforces bugs

hype.heading: Hype vs value: four things a smart contract is not
hype.subtitle: The name oversells it. These four limits matter for every case study later.

cards.title: Not a legal contract
cards.body: It is code that moves assets when conditions are met. Whether a court recognises it is a separate question — most real deployments pair the code with a normal legal agreement.

cards.title: Not smart
cards.body: It does exactly what is written, with no judgement and no exceptions. A bug executes as faithfully as a feature.

cards.title: Not free
cards.body: Every step costs a network fee, and on-chain storage is very expensive: one megabyte on Ethereum costs more than a laptop.

cards.title: Not unstoppable
cards.body: The contract may be, but its website, data feeds and admin keys are ordinary points of control. Tornado Cash's front-end went dark in 2022 while the contract kept running.

value: Removing a middleman that many parties would otherwise have to trust — and pay
Making a rule impossible to bend after the fact — for everyone, including the operator
Settling across borders in seconds, around the clock, with a public audit trail
hype.footer: Ask of every use case: does it need one of these three things? If not, a database will usually win.

keyPoints.s1-warmup: Bitcoin is a ledger for one asset; Ethereum is a shared computer that can run contracts.
keyPoints.s1-recap: A smart contract is an account controlled by code instead of a person.
keyPoints.s1-what: A smart contract turns an agreement into a rule that runs itself.
keyPoints.s1-hype: Not legal, not smart, not free, not unstoppable; the value is removing a middleman, locking a rule and settling fast.
keyPoints.s1-szabo: The vending machine is the whole idea: fixed rules, instant verification, no one to appeal to.
keyPoints.s1-history: Every expensive lesson in thirty years came from code doing exactly what it was told.
keyPoints.s1-exercise: If one trusted institution already runs the process well, a smart contract adds cost, not trust.
